newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine interest rates to survive stk mkt gloom.
newsitem.headline: Philippine interest rates to survive stk mkt gloom.

text.p: Philippine interest rates, raised in recent weeks to ease pressure on the peso from stock market sales, are not likely to sustain their uptrend, bankers and analysts said on Wednesday.

Low inflation, an expected goverment budget surplus and a liquid financial system will be reflected in interest rates when the local equities market finally sobers up which may take one or two months, they said.
In the past seven days, the Philippine Central Bank was forced to raise its key overnight borrowing rate twice by a total of 1.25 percentage points to 11.5 percent.
The action was taken to defend the peso after a crash in the stock market led to fears of capital flight.
The share market was hit following some poor corporate results and a belief the property sector was overheated.

"I think the situation is temporary. Because your hard core inflation is 4 to 5 percent, you cannot have interest rates at 11 to 12 percent - 700 basis points premium over inflation rate. You can't hold that for a long time," said Omar Cruz, vice president of Citibank in Manila.
"Even the market in the long-end does not buy (this view). That's why rates flattened," he added.

The Central Bank's move to quell peso speculation has since resulted in a flat yield curve for domestic interest rates, with the overnight rate nearly close to the average one-year Treasury bill rate of 11.933 percent.
Also, at the auction on Tuesday, the two-year Treasury note fetched an average rate of 11.89 percent, lower than the one year T-bill rate.
T-bill rates, however, are still lower from last year, with the benchmark 91-day rate averaging at 10.108 percent to date from 12.79 percent in the same period last year.
Analysts said the 91-day rate was still on track to meet with full-year projections of 10.5 to 11.0 percent from 12.4 last year.

"In the next two to three weeks, we're just looking at a flattening of the yield curve. We don't expect further increases in the overnight rate in the long term," said Enrico Cruz, treasury head of Deutsche Bank.
"It's too early to say whether it (interest rates) will go up or down (for now)," said Rafael Algarra, vice president of Standard Chartered Bank.
He said the short-term direction of interest rates would depend on how the peso would react to the volatile movements in the stock market.
Manila shares made a smart recovery on the first two days this week but on Wednesday it fell prey to profit-taking.
Deustche Bank's Cruz said foreign investors are likely to wait for the release of the first quarter gross national product in the first week of June before returning.
